questions.q: Which constitutional article originally granted special autonomous status to Jammu & Kashmir, and what was the legal instrument used to abrogate it in August 2019?
questions.a: Article 370 granted special status; it was abrogated through the Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, passed by Parliament under Article 370(3) via a Presidential Order (C.O. 272) and a statutory resolution. A wrong answer (e.g., “Article 371” or “by a simple majority”) reveals confusion between special provisions for different states and the specific procedure for altering J&K’s status.

questions.q: The textbook states: “Democracy allows the political expressions of regional aspirations and does not look upon them as anti-national.” Explain why the Indian model treats regionalism differently from the European model of nation-building.
questions.a: European nation-states historically pursued cultural homogeneity (one language, one culture) and saw diversity as a threat; India’s “salad bowl” nationalism explicitly protects the right of regions to retain distinct cultures (language, script, customs) under Articles 29–30 and the linguistic reorganization of states. A wrong answer that claims “India suppresses regionalism” or “Europe allows more autonomy” shows a failure to grasp the constitutional commitment to unity *with* diversity.

questions.q: A new statehood demand arises in a backward region of an existing state (e.g., Vidarbha in Maharashtra). Using the principles from the chapter, list the constitutional and political steps the Centre should follow to address this demand democratically.
questions.a: Steps: (1) Initiate dialogue with stakeholders (not treat as law-and-order). (2) Set up a commission (like the States Reorganisation Commission) to assess viability — administrative, economic, cultural. (3) If viable, introduce a Bill in Parliament under Article 3 (requires Presidential reference to the concerned state legislature). (4) Ensure power-sharing: the new state gets full federal powers; the parent state’s interests are safeguarded (water, assets). (5) Provide special development packages to address regional imbalance (the root cause). A wrong answer that jumps straight to “send paramilitary forces” or “amend the Constitution immediately” misses the negotiated, federal, and developmental logic of accommodation.

questions.q: Compare the outcomes of the Mizo Accord (1986) and the Punjab Accord (1985). Why did the former achieve lasting peace while the latter saw a decade of continued violence?
questions.a: The Mizo Accord granted full statehood with special protections (Article 371G), integrated the MNF into electoral politics, and addressed the core grievance (alienation from Assam’s neglect). The Punjab Accord conceded Chandigarh and water tribunals but failed to implement them promptly; the Centre’s continued reliance on security forces, delayed justice for 1984 anti-Sikh violence, and factionalisation of Akali Dal eroded trust. A wrong answer focusing only on “Pakistan’s role” ignores the domestic political economy of implementation and power-sharing.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: “The abrogation of Article 370 in 2019 completed the integration of Jammu & Kashmir, resolving the tension between regional autonomy and national unity.” Use evidence from the chapter and subsequent developments.
questions.a: The statement is partially true legally (J&K is now fully under the Indian Constitution) but contested politically. The chapter highlights three Kashmiri grievances: unfulfilled plebiscite promise, erosion of autonomy in practice, and democratic deficit. Abrogation addressed the second by removing special provisions, but the other two remain — democratic processes were suspended (President’s Rule, delimitation, delayed assembly elections), and the plebiscite promise is moot. Lasting unity requires restoring elected government and addressing developmental asymmetry (Ladakh vs. Kashmir vs. Jammu). A wrong answer that calls it “fully resolved” or “completely illegitimate” fails to weigh both constitutional change and democratic legitimacy.

questions.q: Draft a constitutional amendment proposal (in 3–4 clauses) that would create a permanent, institutionalised mechanism for negotiating regional autonomy demands — so that future crises do not require ad hoc accords.
questions.a: A strong proposal would include: (1) A permanent “Regional Aspirations Commission” (constitutional body under Article 263/280) with representatives from states, Centre, and civil society. (2) Mandatory dialogue within 90 days of a verified demand (threshold: 10% of state legislative assembly resolution or 5 lakh signatures). (3) Time-bound implementation of agreed terms, monitored by the Inter-State Council. (4) Special development fund for regions granting autonomy, tied to outcomes. A poor proposal that merely says “give more powers to states” or “ban separatist parties” lacks institutional design and ignores the need for structured negotiation.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ in the Indian context refers to the political assertion of distinct regional identities — linguistic, cultural, ethnic, or economic — within the framework of the Indian Union, seeking greater autonomy, statehood, or resource control.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you see a news headline: “Students in Ladakh demand Union Territory status” or “Bodo groups sign peace accord for Bodoland ______ Region.” These are not isolated events — they are the latest chapter in India’s 75-year experiment of managing regional aspirations through democracy.
What is Regionalism in the Indian context? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Regionalism in the Indian context refers to the political assertion of distinct regional identities — linguistic, cultural, ethnic, or economic — within the framework of the Indian Union, seeking greater autonomy, statehood, or resource control.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you see a news headline: “Students in Ladakh demand Union Territory status” or “Bodo groups sign peace accord for Bodoland Territorial Region.” These are not isolated events — they are the latest chapter in India’s ______-year experiment of managing regional aspirations through democracy.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Regionalism in the Indian context?
questions.a: Students often believe “regionalism = separatism = anti-national” and that the Indian Constitution is rigidly centralised.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how the Indian Constitution’s asymmetric federal design (special provisions, state reorganization, Sixth Schedule) accommodates regional aspirations while preserving national unity, and can evaluate the success and limitations of negotiated settlements (e.g., Punjab Accord, Mizo Accord, Assam Accord) in resolving.
